
A function that silently sums instead of averaging will
pass every rung of the reproducibility ladder and still
be wrong on every machine that runs it. By the end of
this chapter you will be able to say, of any
computational result, whether it has merely been
reproduced or actually checked, and you will have the
four kinds of test, plus a baseline test of the kind
@tbl-baseline-rng demonstrates on the book's own running
cohort, to tell the difference in your own analysis.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 45 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** @sec-levels, for the L0-L3 ladder and
the capture-versus-validation vocabulary this chapter
relies on throughout; @sec-compendium, for the
`inst/tinytest/` layout and the R-package archetype.
Statistically, no more than comfort reading a
coefficient table from a fitted model and a percentile
bootstrap interval; no new statistics are introduced.
R knowledge assumed: writing and calling a function,
vectors, and basic control flow.

**Objectives.** By the end of this chapter, can you:

- state the reproducibility paradox, and explain why
  reproducibility machinery cannot, by itself, detect a
  wrong answer?
- place testing in the validation register rather than
  the capture register, and say what that does and does
  not change about an analysis's position on the L0-L3
  ladder?
- write a unit test, an integration test, a
  data-validation test, and a baseline (reproducibility)
  test in `tinytest`, naming the oracle behind each?
- tell behavioral testing from implementation testing,
  and say why the second kind breaks under an honest
  refactor?
- explain why `lintr`, `styler`, and a pre-commit hook
  belong to the validation register rather than the
  capture register?

**Outline.** The analyst's irreplaceable judgments; the
paradox stated precisely; `tinytest`'s bare-expectation
style; the four kinds of test, worked on the cohort and
the retinopathy trial; behavior versus implementation;
linting, styling, and the pre-commit gate; how the
emphasis shifts across archetypes; a worked example of
the paradox itself; collaborating with an LLM;
exercises, a cheat sheet, and further reading.
:::

## Where this sits on the stack

validation. It is also, among the chapters so far, one
that captures nothing at all: a test suite adds no

## Orientation

Consider a registry study in which an analyst
has written a small function to compute a mean
biomarker value for each treatment arm. The
function carries a quiet bug: it sums the values
but forgets to divide by their count. The
analysis runs without error. It produces a
table, a figure, a p-value. Sent to a colleague,
cloned onto a second machine, restored from a
lockfile inside a pinned container, it runs again
and produces the identical table, the identical
figure, the identical p-value. Every rung of the
ladder of @sec-levels is satisfied: the source is
locatable, the packages are pinned, the
environment is pinned. The result is perfectly
reproducible. It is also perfectly wrong.

This is the reproducibility paradox, and it is
the pivot of this chapter. A buggy function that
returns the wrong answer returns the *same* wrong
answer everywhere, on every machine, at every
later date. Reproducibility machinery, faithfully
applied, does not detect the error; it propagates
it with mechanical fidelity. The lesson, pressed
by Leek and Peng in their aptly titled note that
reproducible research can still be wrong
[@leek2015], is that reproducibility is a floor
and not a ceiling. It guarantees that a result can
be regenerated. It says nothing whatever about
whether the result is correct.

The remedy is testing, and the reason testing
belongs in a book about reproducibility, rather
than in a separate book about software
engineering, is precisely the paradox. Pinning a
package version, building a container, restoring a
lockfile: each of these *captures* a determinant
of the computation, and none of them examines
whether the computation is right. Testing captures
nothing. A test adds no package to the lockfile
and no library to the image. What a test does is
*confirm* that a function, a pipeline, or a dataset
behaves as the analyst intended. It belongs, in the
vocabulary this book has used since @sec-intro, to
the validation register rather than the capture
register, alongside the continuous integration and
output verification of @sec-verification. Capture
fixes the inputs; validation checks that the
fixed inputs still produce the answer they are
supposed to. A reproducible analysis without tests
is trusted; a reproducible analysis with tests is
checked, and the difference between trusting and
checking is the difference this chapter develops.

There is a further and more constructive link to
the ladder. The highest rung, L3 verified, is
reached not by capturing more but by *confirming*
that a recorded computational output regenerates.
That confirmation is itself a test, of a
particular kind we shall meet below as the
baseline test. Testing is therefore not
merely adjacent to the levels; the topmost level
is defined by a test. We begin with the human
judgments that no testing tool can make, then
develop the four kinds of test in turn, then take
up code quality as a second validation feature,
and close with the way the emphasis shifts across
archetypes.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the paradox

A colleague reports that their analysis reaches L2
pinned environment and argues this means the reported
hazard ratio must be correct. What is wrong with the
argument?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

L2 is a claim about capture, that the packages and the
environment are pinned so the same code produces the
same output everywhere. It is not a claim about
correctness: a pinned, containerized analysis still
reproduces a wrong hazard ratio exactly, if the code
that computes it is wrong. Only a test, comparing
against an independent oracle, bears on whether the
number is right.
:::
:::

## The analyst's contribution

Testing tooling runs the checks, tallies the
passes and failures, and reports them. It does not
originate a single one of the judgments that give
a test its value. Three of these judgments are
worth naming at the outset, because they are the
human core of everything that follows.

1. **The analyst decides what 'correct' means.**
   A test compares a computed value against an
   expected one, and the expected one has to come
   from somewhere outside the code under test. This
   source of independent truth is called an oracle:
   a mean of one, two, and three that the analyst
   knows to be two; a count of rows that a data
   dictionary fixes at some known number; a
   coefficient that a textbook formula supplies. No
   tool knows the right answer. The analyst supplies
   it, and a test is only as trustworthy as the
   oracle behind it.

2. **The analyst chooses which behaviors to pin.**
   A function has an infinity of properties, most of
   them incidental to its purpose. The analyst
   decides which few constitute the function's
   contract, the behaviors a future change must not
   break, and writes tests for those. This is the
   distinction, developed below, between testing
   behavior and testing implementation, and it is a
   design judgment, not a mechanical one.

3. **The analyst encodes the domain constraints.**
   The rule that an age lies between zero and one
   hundred and twenty, that a treatment arm is one
   of a fixed set of labels, that a probability sits
   in the unit interval: these are not facts the
   computer can infer. They are clinical and
   scientific knowledge, and a data-validation test
   is the place where that knowledge is written down
   in executable form, so that a violation halts the
   analysis rather than passing silently into a
   result.

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Unit test.** A focused check that one small
  piece of code, typically a single function,
  behaves as intended on known inputs.
- **Integration test.** A check that several
  components behave correctly when composed into a
  pipeline, from raw input to final result.
- **Data-validation test.** A check on the data
  itself rather than the code: that a value lies in
  a plausible range, that no impossible ages appear,
  that the expected columns are present.
- **Reproducibility test.** A check that a recorded
  computational result regenerates. The form that can
  fail is the *baseline test*, which compares a fresh
  result with a value recorded in an earlier session
  and committed, within a stated tolerance; two runs
  in one session do not qualify.
- **Oracle.** The source of independent truth a
  test compares against; the known correct answer.
- **`tinytest`.** A lightweight, zero-dependency R
  testing framework in which a test file is a plain
  script of bare, top-level expectation calls
  [@vanderloo2020].
- **Expectation.** A single assertion, such as
  `expect_equal(actual, expected)`, that passes or
  fails.
- **Linting.** Static analysis of source code for
  stylistic and likely-error patterns, performed by
  `lintr`, without running the code.
- **Styling.** Automatic reformatting of source code
  to a consistent layout, performed by `styler`.
- **Pre-commit hook.** A script that git runs
  automatically before a commit is recorded, used
  here to run the linter and the styler as a gate.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## The reproducibility paradox, stated precisely

It is worth stating the paradox with a little more
care, because its precise form dictates the remedy.
A computational result depends on the code, the
data, and the stack of determinants beneath them
that @sec-levels enumerated. The capture tools of
Part II fix those determinants, so that the
mapping from input to output is held constant
across machines and across time. But holding a
mapping constant says nothing about whether the
mapping is the intended one. If the code encodes
the function 'sum' where the analyst meant the
function 'mean', then capture faithfully preserves
'sum', and every reproduction returns the sum. The
error is not in the reproduction; the reproduction
is flawless. The error is in the mapping, and the
only instrument that examines the mapping is a
test.

Two consequences follow, and they cut in opposite
directions. On the one hand, a result that fails to
reproduce is thereby shown to be untrustworthy,
which is a genuine service; irreproducibility is a
detectable defect. On the other hand, a result that
does reproduce has been shown only to be stable, not
to be right, and stability is easily mistaken for
correctness by an analyst who has watched the same
number appear three times. The paradox is dangerous
exactly because reproduction is so persuasive.
Testing exists to break the false inference from
'it came out the same' to 'it came out correct'.

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

This chapter's own practice reaches a baseline test
on one bootstrap bound (@tbl-baseline-rng) and a short,
illustrative suite of unit, integration, and
data-validation checks on hand-picked examples; it
establishes that those particular results regenerate
and that those particular functions behave as
intended, and it says nothing whatsoever about any
function, dataset, or computation this chapter did not
choose to test.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: capture, faithfully

If the code encodes 'sum' where the analyst meant
'mean', what does capturing the environment do to that
error, and what does it not do?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Capture preserves the error exactly: every reproduction
on every pinned machine returns the same sum, forever.
It does nothing to detect the error, because capture
examines only whether the mapping from input to output
is held constant, never whether the mapping is the
intended one. Only a test, comparing against an
independent oracle, examines the mapping itself.
:::
:::

## The analysis plan as an oracle

The oracle introduced above sits at the level of a
single function: a hand-computed mean, a row count a
data dictionary fixes. The same structure scales up to
the level of the whole analysis's primary result, and
doing so closes a gap the paradox otherwise leaves
open.

A **pre-specified analysis plan** (also called a
statistical analysis plan, or, when it is registered
publicly before the data are seen, a pre-registration)
states in advance the primary endpoint, the model, the
covariates, and the comparison that will answer the
study's main question. Written and dated before the
analyst has looked at the outcome data, it is computed
independently of any code's output in exactly the sense
the Vocabulary box above requires of an oracle: it
specifies what the correct analysis looks like, not by
running anything, but by committing in writing to a
choice that the data cannot later be allowed to revise.

The gap this closes is specific. A function-level
oracle, such as the hand-computed mean described above,
catches a coding error: the function returns the wrong
number for a known input. It says nothing about whether
the analysis itself asks the right question. An analysis
built by trying several models, several covariate sets,
or several endpoints and reporting the one that reached
significance can be bug-free in every function, pass
every unit test, and still reproduce exactly on a second
machine, because reproduction only checks that the same
code returns the same output. The reproducibility
paradox stated above applies again, one level up: a
fully reproducible analysis can still be the wrong
analysis, chosen with the benefit of having already seen
the answer. A pre-specified plan is the oracle that
guards against this failure, because it fixes the
intended analysis before the data could have shaped it.

The two oracles differ in what independence they supply.
A function's oracle is independent of the code that
computes the value; a pre-specified plan is independent
of the data that will later be analyzed. Both are
necessary, and neither substitutes for the other. A
bug-free implementation of an unregistered, data-driven
analysis is still untrustworthy in the way the plan would
have prevented; a faithful implementation of a
pre-specified plan can still contain a coding error that
only a function-level oracle would catch.

In a research compendium, a pre-specified plan is a
dated document, committed to the repository (or
deposited externally, as on the Open Science Framework)
before the raw data arrive, or before they are
unblinded. Checking an analysis against it is not an
`expect_equal()` call but a review step: does the fitted
model's formula, the stated primary comparison, and the
decision rule actually implemented match what the plan
specified? Where the match can be stated mechanically,
for example that `fit_model()` fits the formula the plan
names, a test can assert it directly, comparing the
model's formula (as text, or as a parsed call) against a
string recorded from the plan rather than against
anything the analysis itself computed.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: two oracles

A colleague's bootstrap confidence interval regenerates
bit for bit on a second machine, and every unit test in
the package passes. Is this enough to trust the
reported result as the study's primary finding? What
additional check, and what additional oracle, would you
ask for?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. Reproducing exactly and passing every unit test
shows that the code is a faithful, bug-free
implementation of whatever analysis it runs; neither
check examines whether that analysis is the one the
study committed to before seeing the data. The
additional check is whether the fitted model, the
endpoint, and the comparison match a pre-specified
analysis plan dated before the data arrived. That plan
is the oracle: a source of what the correct analysis
should look like, supplied independently of any result
the code could produce.
:::
:::

## tinytest: bare expectations

The framework this book uses adopts `tinytest`
[@vanderloo2020] as its testing tool, and the
choice rewards a moment's explanation because it
shapes how the tests look. `tinytest` is
lightweight and carries no dependencies of its own,
which matters in a reproducible compendium: every
additional test dependency enlarges the lockfile
and the container image, and a testing framework
that dragged in a dozen packages would tax the very
machinery it is meant to protect. The more visible
consequence is stylistic. A `tinytest` test file is
an ordinary R script containing bare, top-level
expectation calls, with no wrapping function around
them.

A reader who has met `testthat` will notice the
difference at once. Where `testthat` nests each
assertion inside a `test_that('description', {
... })` block, `tinytest` writes the assertion
directly:

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-calculate_mean.R
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(1, 2, 3)), 2)
expect_equal(calculate_mean(5), 5)
expect_true(is.nan(calculate_mean(numeric(0))))
```

Each line is a complete test. The file is also a
runnable script, so during development an analyst
can source it directly and watch the expectations
evaluate. The available expectations cover the
common cases, `expect_equal()`, `expect_true()`,
`expect_false()`, `expect_identical()`,
`expect_error()`, `expect_inherits()`, and a few
others, and a compendium's tests are collected in
`inst/tinytest/` and driven by a small
`tests/tinytest.R` runner that `R CMD check`
invokes. `tinytest` runs each file with the test
directory as its working directory, so a test that
reads a project file from the root reaches it through
`../../`, as the listings below do. We follow the
convention throughout: bare
top-level expectations, one concern per file, named
`test-<thing>.R`.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: reading a bare file

A `tinytest` test file contains no `test_that()` call
and no function definition around its expectations.
What does that tell you about how to run one line of
it during development?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Because each expectation is a bare, top-level

An analyst can `source()` the whole file, or send a
single line to the console, and watch that one
expectation evaluate immediately, with no need to
locate it inside a nested block first.
:::
:::

## The four kinds of test

A research compendium wants four kinds of test, and
they form a progression from the smallest unit of
code to the reproduction of a whole result. We take
them in turn, illustrating each on synthetic data
of the sort a health study might produce.

### Unit tests of functions

A unit test checks that one function behaves as
intended on inputs whose correct outputs are known
independently. The `calculate_mean` function of the
orientation is the canonical case. Its contract is
that it returns the arithmetic mean, and the oracle
is arithmetic done by hand:

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-calculate_mean.R
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(2, 4, 6)), 4)
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(-1, 0, 1)), 0)
expect_true(is.nan(calculate_mean(numeric(0))))
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(1, NA, 3),
                            na.rm = TRUE), 2)
```

The first two lines pin the ordinary behavior
against hand-computed answers. the third and fourth
pin the edge cases, the empty vector and the
missing value, which are exactly the inputs on which
an untested function tends to misbehave. A unit test
suite is, in effect, a written record of what the
analyst believes each function promises.

### Integration tests of the pipeline

A unit test exercises a function in isolation, but a
health analysis is rarely one function. It is a
pipeline, in which raw data is loaded, cleaned,
modeled, and summarized, and the components can be
individually correct yet compose incorrectly. An
integration test runs the pipeline end to end and
checks the result:

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-cohort.R
raw <- load_cohort('../../analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
cohort <- clean_cohort(raw)
fit <- fit_model(cohort)
summary_tbl <- summarise_fit(fit)

expect_inherits(fit, 'lm')
expect_true(all(c('term', 'estimate') %in%
                names(summary_tbl)))
expect_equal(nrow(summary_tbl), 3L)
```

The first expectation looks like a mistake and is not.
`fit_model()` returns a `glm`, because the outcome is
binary, and a `glm` object inherits from `lm`, so the
assertion holds. It is written that way deliberately:
`expect_inherits(fit, 'lm')` pins the contract that the
function returns something the modeling generics will
accept, whereas `expect_equal(class(fit), 'glm')` would
pin the implementation and break the first time the
function was changed to fit a Cox model instead.

The integration test does not re-check what the unit
tests already cover; it checks the seams, that the
output of `clean_cohort` is a valid input to
`fit_model`, that the model summary has the expected
shape. A pipeline that passes its unit tests can
still fail here, if a column is renamed in one step
and read under its old name in the next.

### Data-validation tests

The third kind of test turns its attention from the
code to the data. Much of what goes wrong in a
health analysis is not a coding error but a data
defect: an age of two hundred, a negative
laboratory value, a treatment label misspelled, a
column silently dropped by an upstream export. A
data-validation test encodes the analyst's domain
knowledge as executable constraints and fails when
the data violates them.

Before writing constraints it is worth looking at
what one is constraining. @tbl-diabetic-arms
tabulates the retinopathy trial introduced in the
conventions, and it is included here for a reason
beyond illustration: every cell in it can be counted
by hand from the data, which is precisely the
property an oracle needs. A test asserting that the
untreated arm contains 197 eyes is checkable by
someone who does not trust the function that
produced it. A test asserting that it contains
`nrow(subset(d, trt == 0))` eyes is not a test at
all; it is the function agreeing with itself.


::: {#tbl-diabetic-arms .cell tbl-cap='Eyes and events by treatment arm in the diabetic retinopathy trial (`survival::diabetic`), the real dataset this book computes on. Each count is verifiable by hand from the 394 records, which is what makes the table usable as a test oracle rather than merely as a description.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tibble)
library(knitr)

d <- survival::diabetic
d$arm <- factor(d$trt, levels = c(0, 1),
                labels = c('Untreated', 'Laser'))

arms <- tibble(
  Arm = levels(d$arm),
  Eyes = as.integer(table(d$arm)),
  Events = as.integer(tapply(d$status, d$arm, sum)),
  `Event rate` = sprintf(
    '%.3f', as.numeric(tapply(d$status, d$arm, mean))
  )
)

kable(arms, align = 'lrrr')
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Arm       | Eyes| Events| Event rate|
|:---------|----:|------:|----------:|
|Untreated |  197|    101|      0.513|
|Laser     |  197|     54|      0.274|


:::
:::


The difference between the arms is large and in the
expected direction, which is a reason to be careful
rather than pleased: a validation test should assert
what the protocol requires, not what this particular
extract happens to show. An assertion that the event
rate in the laser arm is below one third would pass
today and would fail on a different trial, or on a
corrected export, for reasons having nothing to do
with a defect. Constraints belong to the protocol,
not to the data in front of you.

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-cohort.R
raw <- load_cohort('../../analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
cohort <- clean_cohort(raw)

# the expected columns are present
expect_true(all(c('mrn', 'age_at_enroll', 'sex', 'incident_dm')
                %in% names(raw)))

# ages lie within the enrollment criteria, not merely
# within the observed range
expect_true(all(cohort$age_at_enroll >= 18 &
                cohort$age_at_enroll <= 105, na.rm = TRUE))

# sex takes only its two coded levels once cleaned
expect_true(all(cohort$sex %in% c('F', 'M')))

# outcome missingness stays within what the analysis
# can tolerate
expect_true(mean(is.na(cohort$incident_dm)) < 0.15)
```

These are the tests that most directly repay a
health scientist, because they catch the errors that
no amount of correct code can prevent, the errors
that live in the data before the analysis begins. In
a data-analysis or simulation archetype, where there
may be few reusable functions to unit-test, the
data-validation tests are often the heart of the
suite.

### Reproducibility tests

The fourth kind closes the loop back to the ladder.
A reproducibility test checks that a recorded result
regenerates. Its most tempting form runs a seeded
procedure twice in one session and asserts that the
two results agree:

```r
# a same-session check: it cannot detect what it
# appears to guard against
expect_equal(bootstrap_ci(cohort, n = 2000, seed = 2024),
             bootstrap_ci(cohort, n = 2000, seed = 2024))
```

Note first where the seed lives. `bootstrap_ci()` takes
it as an argument and sets it internally, with
`withr::with_seed()`, which also restores the caller's
generator state on exit, so the function is
deterministic given its arguments and does not disturb
any random stream around it. A procedure that depends
on the caller setting a seed first is one `set.seed`
away from irreproducible, and moving the seed into the
signature makes forgetting it impossible.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall

A same-session check cannot fail for the reason it
seems to serve. Both calls run in the same R, under the
same random-number defaults, with the same package
versions. When an upgrade changes how `sample()` draws,
as R 3.6.0 did, both calls change together and still
agree. What the check does catch is narrower: a
procedure that ignores its seed. That is worth one line
in a unit test, but it is not a reproducibility test.
:::

A reproducibility test that can fail compares today's
result with one recorded in an earlier session and
committed to the repository. We call it a *baseline
test*, and it has three parts: a script, run once, that
records the baseline; the committed baseline file; and
a test file that recomputes the quantities and compares
them with a stated tolerance.

```r
# analysis/scripts/record_baseline.R
# Run once from the project root, inspect the values,
# then commit the file it writes.
cohort <- clean_cohort(
  load_cohort('analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
)
baseline <- list(
  n_clean = nrow(cohort),
  boot_upper = bootstrap_ci(cohort, n = 2000,
                            seed = 2024)[['upper']],
  r_version = as.character(getRversion()),
  rng_kind = RNGkind()
)
saveRDS(baseline, 'inst/tinytest/baseline-estimates.rds')
```

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-baseline-estimates.R
data_file <- '../../analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'
if (!file.exists(data_file)) {
  exit_file('analysis data absent, as under R CMD check')
}
baseline <- readRDS('baseline-estimates.rds')
cohort <- clean_cohort(load_cohort(data_file))

expect_equal(nrow(cohort), baseline$n_clean,
             info = 'cleaned row count matches the baseline')
expect_equal(
  bootstrap_ci(cohort, n = 2000, seed = 2024)[['upper']],
  baseline$boot_upper, tolerance = 1e-8,
  info = 'seeded bootstrap bound matches the baseline'
)
```

Three details carry the weight. The paths are relative
to `inst/tinytest/`, where `tinytest` runs the file. The
guard lets the file exit quietly under `R CMD check`,
which installs the package without `analysis/`; the
price is that `R CMD check` never runs this test, so the
step that does run it, from the project root, must also
confirm that it ran (@sec-verification). And the
tolerance is stated and chosen, not left at a default.
Given the seed, the sampler, the code, and the data, the
bound is deterministic, so the tolerance is numerical,
not statistical: `1e-8` relative is wide enough to absorb
a floating-point summation reordered by a different BLAS
or thread count (@sec-containers) and far too narrow for
a change in the resampled draws to pass. A comparison
with no tolerance would fail on that reordering, and a
check that fails for reasons unrelated to the analysis
trains its reader to ignore it.

The test can be watched failing for the reason it
exists. The chunk below plays both sessions on the
synthetic cohort. It records the 97.5 percent bootstrap
bound for mean BMI under the sampler R used before
version 3.6.0 (`sample.kind = 'Rounding'`), as an
analysis recorded on an older R would have; reruns it
with the same seed and sampler; and reruns it with the
same seed under the current default (`'Rejection'`). The
comparison is the one `expect_equal()` makes, `all.equal()`
at the stated tolerance. `withr::with_seed()` sets the
sampler only for the duration of each call, and the final
`stopifnot()` confirms the session's generator is as it
was.


::: {#tbl-baseline-rng .cell tbl-cap='A baseline test across sessions. The bound recorded under the pre-3.6.0 sampler is reproduced exactly by a rerun with the same seed and sampler, and is not reproduced by a rerun with the same seed under the current default sampler, so the comparison at tolerance 1e-8 passes once and fails once. A same-session check would have passed in both cases.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(knitr)

cohort <- read.csv('../data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
bmi <- cohort$bmi[!is.na(cohort$bmi)]

boot_upper <- function(x, seed, sample_kind, reps = 2000) {
  withr::with_seed(
    seed,
    {
      means <- replicate(reps, mean(sample(x, replace = TRUE)))
      unname(quantile(means, 0.975))
    },
    .rng_sample_kind = sample_kind
  )
}

kind_before <- RNGkind()[3]

# R warns whenever the pre-3.6.0 sampler is selected;
# the warning is expected here and muffled.
baseline <- suppressWarnings(boot_upper(bmi, 2024, 'Rounding'))
rerun_same <- suppressWarnings(boot_upper(bmi, 2024, 'Rounding'))
rerun_new <- boot_upper(bmi, 2024, 'Rejection')

tol <- 1e-8
passes <- function(current) {
  isTRUE(all.equal(current, baseline, tolerance = tol))
}

checks <- data.frame(
  run = c('recorded baseline (Rounding)',
          'rerun, same seed and sampler (Rounding)',
          'rerun, same seed, current default (Rejection)'),
  upper_bound = c(baseline, rerun_same, rerun_new),
  passes = c('(baseline)',
             ifelse(passes(rerun_same), 'yes', 'no'),
             ifelse(passes(rerun_new), 'yes', 'no'))
)

stopifnot(identical(RNGkind()[3], kind_before))

kable(checks, digits = 4,
      col.names = c('Run', '97.5% bootstrap bound',
                    'Passes at tolerance 1e-8'))
```

## Verification

To see this hold on your own machine: run
`Rscript -e 'tinytest::test_package("mycompendium")'` from
a clean checkout and confirm `test-baseline-estimates.R`
reports a pass (habit 4). To make it fail on purpose,
edit the committed `baseline-estimates.rds` by hand, or
change the seed or `n` passed to `bootstrap_ci()` in
`record_baseline.R` without regenerating the baseline,
and rerun the same test; the comparison above, run with
`sample.kind = 'Rejection'` against a baseline recorded
under `'Rounding'`, is this exact failure captured in the
chapter rather than only described.
:::

A baseline test is what L3 requires. The top rung, as
@sec-levels defines it, asks that recorded outputs be
shown to regenerate within a stated tolerance from a
clean rebuild. The baseline test supplies the recorded
outputs and the tolerance; running it inside an
environment rebuilt from its recipe supplies the clean
rebuild, and @sec-verification assembles the two in
continuous integration. A suite with no baseline test
can show that the code runs and that its functions are
correct on known inputs, but it cannot show that a
recorded result regenerates, so it does not reach L3
however thorough it is. In the zzcollab composition,
`zzc verify --full` applies exactly this rule: it stamps
L3 only when the image rebuilds, the test suite passes,
and at least one `inst/tinytest/test-baseline*.R` file
exists and ran; otherwise it reports the project as
rebuilt and tested, at L2, with no baseline comparison.

## Monte Carlo error and parallel streams

@tbl-baseline-rng fixed the seed and the sampler and
varied only the R version, which isolated one source of
change in the bootstrap bound. A second source is always
present and has nothing to do with R versions: a bootstrap
estimate is itself a Monte Carlo quantity, built from a
finite number of resamples, and it carries its own
sampling variability on top of the statistical sampling
variability of the original cohort. Two bootstrap runs at
different seeds, same data, same `n`, will not return
exactly the same bound, and the size of that disagreement
is the Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE), distinct from
the standard error the bootstrap is estimating.

The practical diagnostic needs no extra theory: rerun the
same call at several seeds for a given `n`, and look at
how much the result moves; then raise `n` and watch the
spread narrow. The chunk below does this with
`bootstrap_ci()` on the HbA1c odds ratio, at `n = 300` and
`n = 1500`, three seeds each.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cohort <- clean_cohort(
  load_cohort('../../analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
)
width <- function(n, seed) {
  ci <- bootstrap_ci(cohort, n = n, seed = seed)
  unname(ci['upper'] - ci['lower'])
}
w300 <- vapply(1:3, width, numeric(1), n = 300)
w1500 <- vapply(1:3, width, numeric(1), n = 1500)
```
:::


At `n = 300` the interval's width across the three seeds
ranges over 3.50 to
4.13, a standard deviation of
0.319. At `n = 1500`, five times
as many resamples, the same spread falls to
0.101, a reduction broadly
consistent with the Monte Carlo error's usual
$1/\sqrt{n}$ scaling, though three seeds is too few to
pin the exponent down. A result is 'Monte Carlo stable'
at a given comparison tolerance when this seed-to-seed
spread is small relative to that tolerance; the baseline
test's `1e-8` in @tbl-baseline-rng is a numerical
tolerance for one fixed sequence of draws and says
nothing about this, so raising `n` until the spread
shown here is small relative to whatever difference the
analysis cares about detecting is a separate check,
made once, by hand, when choosing `n`, not by the test
suite on every run.

Resampling at the `n` a real analysis needs is often
parallelized across cores, and this is where Monte Carlo
error becomes a correctness risk rather than only a
precision question. Each worker process must draw from
its own independent random stream; naive parallelization,
such as `parallel::mclapply()` with no RNG setup, can
leave workers sharing or overlapping generator state, so
that resamples drawn as 'independent' on different cores
are correlated, which understates the Monte Carlo error
rather than merely adding to it. The fix is the
L'Ecuyer-CMRG generator, built for exactly this, which
R's `RNGkind('L\'Ecuyer-CMRG')` exposes directly and which
`parallel::clusterSetRNGStream()` applies across the
workers of a cluster, assigning each one a non-overlapping
substream; the `doRNG` package applies the same discipline
to a `foreach` loop. A parallel bootstrap run without this
is not merely imprecise; its reported width can understate
the true Monte Carlo error, and it adds a second way for
the result to depend on how many cores happened to run it,
on top of the seed discipline this chapter already
requires.

and does increasing `n` fix both?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. The seed-to-seed change at fixed `n` is Monte Carlo
error, the resampling's own finite-sample noise; raising
`n` shrinks it toward zero. The sampler change after an
upgrade is a change in which resamples a *given* seed
produces, not in how many resamples were drawn; raising
`n` does not fix it, because the two samplers will keep
disagreeing at any `n`. Only pinning the sampler, as the
baseline test does, addresses that second problem.
:::
:::

The four kinds are not four ways of doing one thing.

## Test behavior, not implementation

A test is worth writing only if it survives changes
that ought not to break it and fails on changes that
ought to. The way to secure this is to test what a
function does, its observable behavior, rather than
how it does it, its internal implementation. The
distinction is easiest to see in a pair of tests for
the same function:

```r
# fragile: pins an implementation detail
expect_true('filter' %in% all.names(body(my_clean)))

# robust: pins the behavior
result <- my_clean(data.frame(x = c(1, NA, 3)))
expect_false(anyNA(result))
```

The first test asserts that `my_clean` uses a
function called `filter` internally. If the analyst
later rewrites `my_clean` in base R, removing the
`filter` call while leaving its behavior
unchanged, the first test fails, and it fails for no
good reason: the function still does exactly what it
promised. Such a test punishes honest refactoring
and trains the analyst to distrust the suite. The
second test asserts only that the cleaned data
carries no missing values, which is the behavior
that actually matters, and it passes under any
correct implementation. As a general rule, a test
should fail when, and only when, the function's
contract is broken. Tests that fail for other
reasons are a tax on maintenance, and Wilson and
colleagues, in their best-practices and
good-enough-practices guidance, make behavioral
testing a recurring recommendation [@wilson2014;
@wilson2017].

A corollary concerns how much to test. A test that
merely confirms a result is a data frame, without
checking any value in it, tests too little and gives
false comfort. A test that pins every incidental
property tests too much and breaks on every
revision. The judgment of what to pin, named above
as the second of the analyst's contributions, is the
skill the tooling cannot supply.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## Code quality as a validation feature

Testing confirms that code is correct. A second
family of tools confirms that code is *legible and
consistent*, and although these tools do not check
correctness directly, they belong to the same
validation register and serve the same
reproducibility end. The argument is one of
mechanism. Code that a reader can follow is code
whose errors a reader can find; consistent
formatting removes the visual noise that hides a
transposed argument or a misplaced parenthesis; and
a single house style across a compendium means that
a difference in the code is always a difference in
meaning, never merely a difference in whitespace.
Wilson and colleagues, in both of their practice
papers, treat readable, conventional code as a
component of reproducible work rather than an
aesthetic preference [@wilson2014; @wilson2017];
Sandve and colleagues, in their ten simple rules,
make the companion point that the provenance and the
recorded results of an analysis must themselves be
preserved [@sandve2013].

Two tools mechanize this, and a third enforces them.

**Linting** is static analysis: `lintr` reads the
source without running it and flags stylistic
deviations and likely errors, an assignment with
`=` where the house style is `<-`, a line past the
width limit, a variable assigned and never used, a
call to a function that does not exist. Because it
does not execute the code, it catches a class of
mistake that tests, which only exercise the paths
they call, may miss.

**Styling** is automatic reformatting: `styler`
rewrites the source into a consistent layout,
fixing indentation, spacing, and alignment, so that
formatting is never a matter for human attention or
for a code review. The two are complementary;
`styler` fixes the formatting that `lintr` would
otherwise complain about.

In the framework, both run inside the project
container through Makefile targets, so that no host
R installation is required and every collaborator
runs the identical checks:

```bash
$ make style   # reformat R code with styler
$ make lint    # analyze R code with lintr
```

**A pre-commit hook** enforces them. A hook is a
script that git runs automatically at a defined
moment; a pre-commit hook runs before a commit is
recorded, and can refuse the commit if a check
fails. Configuring the linter and styler as a
pre-commit hook means that unstyled or unlinted code
cannot enter the history in the first place, which
is a far stronger guarantee than a convention that
relies on the analyst's memory. The configuration
lives in a `.pre-commit-config.yaml` file at the
project root:

```yaml
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/lorenzwalthert/precommit
    rev: v0.4.3
    hooks:
      - id: style-files
      - id: lintr
      - id: readme-rmd-rendered
      - id: no-browser-statement
```

With this in place, an attempt to commit code that
`styler` would reformat, or that `lintr` flags, or
that contains a stray `browser()` left over from
debugging, is stopped before the commit completes,
and the analyst is prompted to fix it. Continuous
integration, in @sec-verification, runs the same
checks again on the server, so that a collaborator
who has not installed the hook is caught
nonetheless. The hook is the fast local gate; CI is
the authoritative remote one.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## Validation in the regulated sense

Every use of 'validation' in this chapter has been the
statistical and software-engineering sense: checking that
code is correct, that data meet a constraint, that a
result regenerates. In pharmaceutical, medical-device, and
other FDA- or EMA-regulated work, 'validation' names a
narrower and more procedural idea, and @sec-levels's
warning box introduces the distinction; this section
develops the three practices that fill it out for testing
specifically.

**Computer system validation.** Under 21 CFR 11.10(a),
a regulated electronic record system must be validated
'to ensure accuracy, reliability, consistent intended
performance, and the ability to discriminate invalid or
altered records' [@cfr21part11], a standard reflected in
parallel form in European Medicines Agency expectations
for computerized systems in the same regulatory setting.
This is validation of the system across its lifecycle,
documented once and maintained by a change-control
process, not a one-time test run. A `tinytest` suite that
passes is evidence toward this standard; it is not, by
itself, the standard, which also demands documented
installation qualification, operational qualification,
and a record of who approved each change and when.

**Double programming.** Independent of any code-based
test, a regulated submission is commonly checked by
*double programming*: two analysts, or one analyst and an
independent reviewer, implement the same analysis
separately, from the same specification, usually in
isolation from each other's code, and the two results are
compared. This is a different reproducibility practice
from everything else in this chapter. A baseline test
reruns the *same* code and checks that it still returns
the same answer; double programming runs *two different*
implementations of the same specification and checks that
they agree. A bug shared by both implementations, because
both analysts misread the same ambiguous protocol
sentence, would pass a baseline test (the code is
unchanged) and would also pass double programming (the
two analysts made the same mistake); what double
programming catches is a bug particular to one
implementation, the error a single analyst's code review
is least likely to find in their own work.

**Package risk assessment.** Pinning package versions,
as @sec-dependencies teaches, fixes which code runs; it
says nothing about how much to trust that code. The R
Validation Hub, an R Consortium working group formed for
exactly this question, proposes a risk-based answer
[@nicholls2020]: classify each package as either
'intended for use' (called directly by the analysis) or
an unexamined dependency reached only through another
package; for each intended-for-use package, assess its
purpose, maintenance practice, community usage, and
existing test coverage; and have a qualified reviewer
record a documented risk judgment, higher risk earning
additional targeted testing and lower risk, such as base
R or a long-established tidyverse package, earning
'trusted' status with no further work. The `riskmetric`
package operationalizes several of these metrics so the
assessment does not start from nothing. This is a
judgment about trustworthiness layered on top of the
pinning @sec-dependencies already does, not a replacement
for it.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

## Testing across the archetypes

The four kinds of test are the same in every
compendium, but their relative weight shifts with
the archetype, and it is worth making the shift
explicit, because a student who has met testing only
in the context of R packages may wrongly conclude
that a data analysis has nothing to test.

Testing is native to the **R-package** archetype.
The package is the setting in which the machinery
grew up: tests live in a conventional directory,
`R CMD check` runs them as a matter of course, and
the whole apparatus of unit testing was designed
around functions with clean inputs and outputs. A
package's suite is dominated by unit tests, because
a package is mostly a collection of functions, and
the universal gate that @sec-compendium described,
`R CMD check`, exercises them on every build.

The **data-analysis** and **simulation** archetypes
are where testing is less conventional and, for that
reason, most in need of emphasis. Such a compendium
may contain few reusable functions and no exported
interface, so the unit-test surface is small. Its
risk lives elsewhere: in the data, which may be
malformed, and in the result, which must
regenerate. Here the data-validation tests and the
reproducibility tests carry the weight. A simulation
archetype in particular leans on the reproducibility
test, because its entire output is a function of a
seed, and a baseline test that fixes the seed and
compares the result with the committed baseline is the
guarantee that the reported numbers can be recovered.
The point developed at length in
@sec-verification, that seeding is the load-bearing
determinant of a simulation, has its testing
counterpart exactly here.

The **manuscript** archetype adds one further
concern, that the rendered report itself continues
to build, which sits between testing and the
literate-programming machinery of @sec-literate; a
test that the report renders, and that its headline
numbers match a baseline, guards the paradox at the
level of the whole document.

The **blog** archetype tests the code that its posts
depend on. A teaching blog whose posts contain
runnable examples has a reproducibility obligation
to its readers no smaller than a manuscript's to its
reviewers: a code snippet that no longer runs, or
that now returns a different number than the prose
around it claims, is a published error. Testing the
functions and the example computations that the
posts rely on is how a blog keeps that promise
across the many posts it renders. In every
archetype, then, the tests are drawn from the same
four kinds; what changes is which kinds bear the
load.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}

`tinytest` package, which may be absent from a bare R
session, we hand-roll a one-line expectation, which
is all a bare check really is: a comparison of an
actual value against an expected one.


::: {#tbl-paradox .cell tbl-cap='A correct function and a buggy variant checked against three inputs with hand-computed means. The buggy variant returns the same wrong value on every input and would return it on every machine and every rerun: it is perfectly reproducible and still wrong.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
# the function under test, in a correct and a
# buggy form
calculate_mean <- function(x, na.rm = FALSE) {
  if (na.rm) x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  sum(x) / length(x)
}

calculate_mean_buggy <- function(x) {
  sum(x)                 # bug: division dropped
}

# a minimal hand-rolled expectation: no testing
# package required
expect <- function(actual, expected, tol = 1e-8) {
  isTRUE(abs(actual - expected) < tol)
}

# three inputs whose means are known independently
cases <- list(c(1, 2, 3),
              c(10, 20, 30, 40),
              c(5, 5, 5, 5, 5))
oracle <- c(2, 25, 5)

results <- data.frame(
  input = vapply(cases,
                 function(x) paste(x, collapse = ', '),
                 character(1)),
  expected = oracle,
  correct = vapply(cases, calculate_mean, numeric(1)),
  buggy = vapply(cases, calculate_mean_buggy,
                 numeric(1))
)
results$correct_passes <-
  mapply(expect, results$correct, oracle)
results$buggy_passes <-
  mapply(expect, results$buggy, oracle)

knitr::kable(results)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|input          | expected| correct| buggy|correct_passes |buggy_passes |
|:--------------|--------:|-------:|-----:|:--------------|:------------|
|1, 2, 3        |        2|       2|     6|TRUE           |FALSE        |
|10, 20, 30, 40 |       25|      25|   100|TRUE           |FALSE        |
|5, 5, 5, 5, 5  |        5|       5|    25|TRUE           |FALSE        |


:::
:::


The table records the whole of the lesson. The
correct function passes every check; the buggy
function fails every check, and it fails them
identically. Were we to rerun this chunk a thousand
times, on a thousand machines, the `buggy` column
would hold the same wrong values every time. The bug
is not a source of variability, which reproducibility
tooling might eventually surface; it is a source of
constant, faithful, reproducible error, which only a
comparison against an independent oracle can catch.
That comparison is what a test is.

In a real compendium, the hand-rolled `expect` gives
way to the `tinytest` expectations, and the checks
live in a file under `inst/tinytest/`. The following
is that file, shown as a static listing rather than
run here, and it is exactly the unit test that would
have caught the bug before it reached a result:

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-calculate_mean.R
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(1, 2, 3)), 2)
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(10, 20, 30, 40)), 25)
expect_equal(calculate_mean(rep(5, 5)), 5)
expect_true(is.nan(calculate_mean(numeric(0))))
expect_equal(calculate_mean(c(1, NA, 3),
                            na.rm = TRUE), 2)
```

The runner `tests/tinytest.R` that `R CMD check`
invokes is a three-line file:

```r
# tests/tinytest.R
if (requireNamespace('tinytest', quietly = TRUE)) {
  tinytest::test_package('mycompendium')
}
```

and the pre-commit configuration shown earlier
completes the picture: the linter and styler guard
the code's legibility on every commit, the tinytest
suite guards its correctness, and continuous
integration re-runs both on a clean machine so that
neither guarantee depends on the author's local
setup.

## Check your understanding: the oracle in the table

In @tbl-paradox, why is `oracle <- c(2, 25, 5)` written
by hand in the chunk rather than computed by calling
`calculate_mean()` on the three `cases`?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Because an oracle has to come from outside the code
under test. Computing the expected values by calling
`calculate_mean()` would make the check compare the
function against itself; it would pass identically
whether `calculate_mean` were correct or carried the
dropped-division bug, since both forms are internally
consistent with their own output. The hand-written
vector is what lets the table show the buggy column
failing every row.
:::
:::

## Collaborating with an LLM

A language model is a capable assistant for writing
tests, and a dangerous one for a specific reason: it
will readily produce tests that pass, which is not
the same as tests that are correct. The analyst's
verification duty is heaviest exactly where the
model is most fluent.

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

Tests sit close to the data, so one rule comes first
(habit 3). Never paste or upload protected health
information, identifiable records, or data covered by a
data-use agreement, nor outputs derived from them, such
as a failing test's printout of offending rows, into a
model unless your institution has approved that endpoint
for that data. Describe the structure instead: the data
dictionary, column names and types, and a synthetic
example such as the book's simulated cohort. A coding
agent reads the files in its project, so run one only
where it is permitted to see the data.
:::

**Prompt.** 'Here is my `calculate_mean` function.
Write `tinytest` unit tests for it, including edge
cases.'

*Watch for.* A model tends to derive the expected
values by running the function it was given, rather
than by independent computation. If the function is
buggy, the model may generate an oracle that
matches the bug, producing tests that pass against
wrong behavior and thereby certifying the error.
It may also test only the paths the code obviously
takes and miss the empty vector or the missing
value.

*Verification.* Check every expected value by hand
or from an independent formula, not by running the
function. The oracle must come from outside the code
under test; that is the whole point of an oracle.
Confirm that the edge cases you care about, the
empty input, the single value, the missing value,
each have a test.

**Prompt.** 'Here is the data dictionary, not the
data, for my cohort: `age_at_enroll` (integer, years),
`sex` (character, coded `F` or `M` after cleaning),
`bmi` (numeric, kg/m^2), `incident_dm` (integer, 0 or
1). Write `tinytest` data-validation tests for a data
frame with these columns.'

*Watch for.* The model will propose generic checks,
non-missing identifiers, numeric outcomes, that are
reasonable but do not encode *your* domain. The
dictionary gives types and codes; it does not give
the protocol's eligibility ages, the plausible range
of BMI in your population, or how much outcome
missingness the analysis can tolerate, so the model
will invent those bounds.

*Verification.* Supply the domain constraints
yourself, or check that the generated ranges match
your data dictionary. A validation test asserting a
plausible-looking but wrong range is worse than no
test, because it lends false authority.

**Prompt.** 'Explain why this test is failing.'

*Watch for.* The model may recommend changing the
test to match the current output, which makes the
failure disappear without establishing whether the
code or the test was wrong. A failing test is
sometimes correct: it may be reporting a real bug.

*Verification.* Decide first, from the oracle,
whether the code or the expectation is at fault, and
only then change the one that is wrong. Never
silence a failing test by editing its expected value
to whatever the code currently returns; that
converts a test into a tautology.

## Exercise 1

The form of the answer matters more than the function
chosen. For a hypothetical `summarize_visits()`:

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-summarize_visits.R
expect_equal(summarize_visits(c(2, 4, 6)), 4)
expect_true(is.nan(summarize_visits(numeric(0))))
expect_error(summarize_visits('a'))
```

**Where each expected value came from** is the substance of
the exercise, and the three answers should be different.

The ordinary case comes from **arithmetic done by hand**,
independently of the function. This is what makes it an
oracle: if the expected value were computed by running the
function, the test would assert only that the function
agrees with itself, which is the commonest way a test
suite becomes worthless.

The empty-input case comes from **a decision about the
contract**. There is no arithmetic to do; the analyst must
decide what the function should do with no data and then
encode the decision. The test is as much a specification
as a check.

The wrong-type case comes from **the same contract**,
asserting that the function refuses input it cannot
handle rather than returning something misleading.

A reader who finds they cannot state where an expected
value came from has usually written a change-detector
rather than a test.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

The bug is the dropped division, so the function returns a
sum where a mean is intended:

```r
summarize_visits <- function(x) sum(x)   # bug
```

The analysis still runs, produces a number, and produces
the *same* number on every machine and every rerun. If the
project is containerized and its packages pinned, that
number is perfectly reproducible.

The catching test is the ordinary case from exercise 1:

```r
expect_equal(summarize_visits(c(2, 4, 6)), 4)
```

It fails immediately, returning 12 against an expected 4.

**Why reproduction did not catch it.** Because reproduction
asks whether the same inputs give the same outputs, and
they do. The buggy function is deterministic; nothing about
it varies between machines or over time. Reproducibility
machinery captures determinants and propagates whatever
the code computes with mechanical fidelity, including the
wrong thing. The only way to detect the error is to compare
the output against a value obtained *independently of the
code*, which is what the hand-computed oracle supplies and
what no amount of environment capture can.

This is the reproducibility paradox in one line: capture
fixes the inputs, and validation checks that the fixed
inputs produce the intended answer.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

The four constraints, in the form the chapter uses:

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-data-cohort.R
cohort <- readRDS('../../analysis/data/derived_data/cohort.rds')

expect_true(
  all(c('id', 'age', 'sex', 'outcome') %in% names(cohort)),
  info = 'the expected columns are present'
)
expect_true(
  all(cohort$age >= 18 & cohort$age <= 105, na.rm = TRUE),
  info = 'age lies within the enrolled range'
)
expect_true(
  all(cohort$sex %in% c('F', 'M', 'Other')),
  info = 'sex takes only coded levels'
)
expect_true(
  mean(is.na(cohort$outcome)) < 0.05,
  info = 'outcome missingness stays under five percent'
)
```

**The justifications** are the point, and each should come
from outside the data.

The **column set** comes from the data dictionary: these
are the variables the analysis consumes, and a missing one
means an upstream export changed. The **age range** comes
from the protocol's eligibility criteria, not from the
observed minimum and maximum; deriving the bound from the
data would make the test unable to detect the very
excursion it exists to catch. The **label set** comes from
the coding sheet. The **missingness bound** comes from
what the analysis can tolerate before its conclusions
become unsafe, which is a judgment the analyst must make
and record.

The recurring discipline: a range read off the current
data is a description, and a range read off the protocol
is a test.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 4

**All of them belong to the validation register.** Unit
tests and data-validation tests alike pin no determinant:
they add no package to the lockfile and no library to the
image. They confirm that what was captured behaves as
intended.

**What removing them would change.** Nothing about the
position on the L0 to L3 ladder. An analysis at L2 with a
full test suite and the same analysis at L2 with no tests
sit on the same rung, because the rung grades how far down
the determinant stack the result is locked, and tests lock
nothing.

**What removing them would change instead** is whether
anyone has reason to believe the result is right. The
analysis becomes trusted rather than checked, and the
class of error the tests were catching, a wrong function
and an out-of-range dataset, returns to being invisible.

The one qualification worth making, because it is a real
subtlety rather than a hedge, concerns L3. L3 requires that
recorded outputs be shown to regenerate within a stated
tolerance from a clean rebuild, and the evidence for that
is a baseline test. The unit and data-validation tests of
exercises 1 and 3 are not baseline tests, so removing them
leaves L3 where it was; removing the baseline test would
drop a project from L3 to L2, because the one piece of
evidence the rung requires would be gone. It is the
*verification role* that matters there, not the testing
role, and a reader who makes this distinction has
understood the chapter's central division.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 5

```r
# once, from the project root, to record the baseline
cohort <- clean_cohort(
  load_cohort('analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
)
saveRDS(coef(fit_model(cohort)),
        'inst/tinytest/baseline-coefs.rds')
```

```r
# inst/tinytest/test-baseline-coefs.R
data_file <- '../../analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'
if (!file.exists(data_file)) exit_file('no analysis data')
baseline <- readRDS('baseline-coefs.rds')
cohort <- clean_cohort(load_cohort(data_file))
current <- coef(fit_model(cohort))
expect_equal(current, baseline, tolerance = 1e-8,
             info = 'model coefficients match the baseline')
```

The model fit draws no random numbers, so no seed is
needed; a stochastic quantity would take its seed as an
argument, as `bootstrap_ci()` does in the chapter. The
file name begins `test-baseline`, the convention by which
a verification step finds baseline tests. Changing one
line of the analysis makes the test fail, reporting the
coefficients that moved.

**On the tolerance**, which is the part of this exercise
that repays thought. An exact comparison is the strongest
check and will produce failures that mean nothing:
floating-point summation reorders under a different BLAS
or a different thread count, as @sec-containers discusses,
and the last digits move without the analysis changing. A
tolerance of `1e-8` accepts that noise and still catches
any change large enough to alter a reported figure. A
tolerance set too loosely stops detecting real changes,
and there is no universally correct value; it should be
chosen against the precision at which results are
reported.

**What this test is and is not.** It is the kind of
baseline test L3 requires, and it is a *change detector*: it
asserts that today's answer matches the recorded one, not
that either is correct. It is worth being clear about
this, because the baseline was produced by the same code
it now guards. If the code was wrong when the baseline was
recorded, this test will faithfully defend the wrong
answer, which is the paradox reappearing one level up.
The unit tests of exercise 1 are what establish
correctness; this test establishes stability.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 6

**What the hook does.** The commit is refused. The
formatting hook rewrites the offending files in place and
aborts, so the commit does not complete and the working
tree now contains the reformatted code, which must be
staged and committed again. The effect is that
misformatted code cannot enter the history at all.

**The contrast with continuous integration.** CI would let
the commit through. The code enters the history, the push
succeeds, and the check runs afterward on the server,
reporting a failure against a commit that already exists.
Fixing it requires a second commit, so the history now
records both the violation and its repair.

The differences worth naming are three. **Timing:** the
hook acts before the record is written, CI after.
**Locality:** the hook runs on the analyst's machine and
can therefore be skipped, with `--no-verify` or by a
collaborator who never installed it, whereas CI runs on
the server and cannot. **Scope:** the hook must be fast
enough to sit inside a commit, so it does cheap things
like formatting and linting, whereas CI can rebuild the
container and run the full suite.

The two are complements rather than alternatives, and the
chapter's framing explains why: the hook is a convenience
that keeps trivia out of the history, and CI is the gate
that actually guarantees anything, because it is the one
nobody can skip.
:::

## Exercise 8

The code must be committed first, then
`record_baseline.R` is run against that committed code,
and the baseline file it writes is committed second, in
its own commit. This is habit 1 applied to a derived
artifact rather than to the primary analysis: a committed
file must always be traceable to the committed code that
produced it.

Reversing the order breaks that traceability. If the
baseline is regenerated and committed while the code
change that motivated it is still uncommitted, a
collaborator who pulls the repository receives the new
baseline paired with the *old* code, because the code
change never reached the shared history. Their copy of
the baseline test then fails immediately, not because
anything is wrong with their checkout, but because the
repository itself never recorded a consistent pair of
code and baseline. Worse, if the local, uncommitted code
change is later lost, the committed baseline becomes
orphaned: a recorded result with no committed code that
anyone can point to as having produced it, which is
exactly the provenance gap habit 1 exists to close.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Command or rule | What it does |
|---|---|
| `expect_equal(a, e)` | Compares `a` to oracle `e` with `all.equal()`'s default tolerance. |
| `expect_equal(a, e, tolerance = 1e-8)` | The baseline-test comparison: a stated, not default, tolerance (habit 5). |
| `expect_true()`, `expect_false()`, `expect_identical()`, `expect_error()`, `expect_inherits()` | The common `tinytest` expectations beyond equality. |
| `tinytest::test_package('pkg')` | Runs the suite under `inst/tinytest/` via the `tests/tinytest.R` runner. |
| `exit_file('message')` | Exits a test file quietly, for a test that needs data `R CMD check` does not install. |
| `make lint` / `make style` | Run `lintr` / `styler` inside the project container. |
| `test-baseline*.R` naming | The convention `zzc verify --full` looks for to certify L3. |
| Rule of thumb | Test behavior, not implementation; a test should fail only when the contract breaks. |
| Rule of thumb | An oracle must be computed independently of the code under test, never by calling it. |
| Habit 4 | Make every gate able to fail, and watch it fail once. |
| Habit 5 | Compare against a recorded baseline, with a stated tolerance. |

## Further reading

The single most important reference for this chapter
is the short note by Leek and Peng, that reproducible
research can still be wrong [@leek2015], which states
the paradox that motivates every test in a compendium
and argues for a prevention-oriented rather than a
correction-oriented stance toward analytical error.

For the testing tool itself, van der Loo's
documentation of `tinytest` [@vanderloo2020] explains
the design rationale for a zero-dependency,
bare-expectation framework, and is worth reading for
the argument that a testing framework should not
itself be a heavy dependency.

For the practice of testing and code quality as
components of scientific computing rather than as
software-engineering appendages, the two papers by
Wilson and colleagues are the standard references:
the best-practices paper [@wilson2014] and the
good-enough-practices paper [@wilson2017], the latter
pitched deliberately at researchers without a
software background. Sandve and colleagues' ten
simple rules [@sandve2013] cover the same ground in a
compact, rule-by-rule form, and situate readable code
and recorded results within a general reproducibility
discipline.

For the connection between testing and the highest
rung of the ladder, the reader is referred forward to
@sec-verification, where the reproducibility test of
this chapter reappears at the scale of the whole
compendium as output verification, and to @sec-levels
for the capture-and-validation distinction that places
testing in the validation register. Peng's early
account of reproducibility as a spectrum [@peng2011]
remains the clearest short statement of why confirming
a result, and not merely producing it, is a minimum
scientific standard.
